function_description: Return the gradient of an N-dimensional array.
parameters: f: array_like, An N-dimensional array containing samples of a scalar function.
varargs: list of scalar or array, optional. Spacing between f values. Default unitary spacing for all dimensions.
axis: None or int or tuple of ints, optional. Gradient is calculated only along the given axis or axes.
edge_order: {1, 2}, optional. Gradient is calculated using N-th order accurate differences at the boundaries. Default: 1.
update_info: return type changed from list to tuple
update_description: The numpy.gradient function now returns a tuple instead of a list, making the return value immutable.
code_example:
import numpy as np
f = np.array([1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 16], dtype=float)
np.gradient(f)

function_description: Computes the one-dimensional discrete Fourier Transform using the Fast Fourier Transform algorithm.

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Length of the transformed axis of the output. If smaller than the input, it is cropped; if larger, padded with zeros. Default is the input's length along the specified axis.

parameters.name: axis
parameters.description: Axis over which to compute the FFT. Default is the last axis.

parameters.name: out
parameters.description: Output array where the result will be placed. Must be of the appropriate shape and dtype.

note: FFT is most efficient when n is a power of two. The DFT is defined with conventions described in the numpy.fft documentation.
update_description: The numpy.fft.fft function now supports an 'out' parameter for in-place calculations, allowing the result to be stored in a pre-allocated array.
code_example:
import numpy as np
result = np.fft.fft(x, out=preallocated_array)

function_description: Returns the least-squares solution to a linear matrix equation, handling under-, well-, or over-determined systems.

parameters.name: b
parameters.description: Ordinate or dependent variable values. If b is two-dimensional, the least-squares solution is calculated for each of the K columns of b.

parameters.name: rcond
parameters.description: Cut-off ratio for small singular values of a.

return type: tuple of ndarrays (x, residuals, rank, s)
update_description: The default rcond value for numpy.linalg.lstsq has been updated to machine precision times max(M, N).
code_example:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[0., 1.], [1., 1.], [2., 1.], [3., 1.]])
y = np.array([-1, 0.2, 0.9, 2.1])
x = np.linalg.lstsq(A, y, rcond=None)
print(x[0])

function_description: Checks if a cast between data types is possible based on the specified casting rule.

parameters.name: from_
parameters.description: dtype, dtype specifier, NumPy scalar, or array to cast from.

parameters.name: to
parameters.description: dtype or dtype specifier to cast to.

parameters.name: casting
parameters.description: {‘no’, ‘equiv’, ‘safe’, ‘same_kind’, ‘unsafe’}, optional. Controls what kind of data casting may occur.

update_info: parameter change: cannot be called on Python int, float, or complex
update_description: numpy.can_cast cannot be called with Python int, float, or complex instances as the result must not depend on the value passed in.
code_example:
import numpy as np
result = np.can_cast(np.int32, np.float64)

function_description: Clips (limits) the values in an array to a specified interval, replacing values outside the interval with the interval's edges.
note: When min is greater than max, clip returns an array in which all values are equal to max.
update_info: Parameter names changed from a_min/a_max to min/max
update_description: In numpy.clip, the parameters max and min are meant to replace a_min and a_max. Additionally, calling np.clip(a) or np.clip(a, None, None) now returns a copy of the input array instead of raising an error.
code_example: import numpy as np; a = np.arange(10); print(np.clip(a, 1, 8))

function_description: Gives a new shape to an array without changing its data.

parameters.name: shape
parameters.description: int or tuple of ints The new shape should be compatible with the original shape.

parameters.name: newshape
parameters.description: int or tuple of ints Deprecated since version 2.1: Replaced by shape argument. Retained for backward compatibility.

parameters.name: order
parameters.description: {‘C’, ‘F’, ‘A’}, optional Read the elements of a using this index order...

parameters.name: copy
parameters.description: bool, optional If True, then the array data is copied.

note: It is not always possible to change the shape of an array without copying the data. The order keyword gives the index ordering both for fetching the values from a and placing the values into the output array.
update_description: The numpy.reshape function now supports the shape and copy parameters, allowing for more flexible array reshaping.

function_description: Converts the input to an ndarray, passing through ndarray subclasses without copying if possible.
note: The 'device' parameter is for Array-API interoperability and must be 'cpu' if passed. The 'copy' parameter was introduced in version 2.1.0, and 'like' in version 1.20.0.
update_description: The numpy.asanyarray function now supports the copy and device parameters, matching the behavior of asarray.

function_description: A context manager for setting print options temporarily and restoring them upon exit.
note: The as-clause of the with-statement can capture the previous print options.
update_description: The numpy.printoptions function now supports the override_repr parameter for defining custom repr(array) behavior.
code_example:
import numpy as np
with np.printoptions(precision=2):
    print(np.array([2.0])/3)

function_description: Copies an array to a specified data type.
note: array_likes are explicitly not supported here. The device parameter is for Array-API interoperability and must be 'cpu' if passed. When copy=False and dtype matches input dtype, the input array is returned.
update_description: The numpy.astype function now supports the device parameter for specifying the device on which the array should be placed.
